title: Job 30:1–15
context: Job turns from the past with “But now” (30:1). Those younger than he now mock him, sons of men whom he describes as gaunt with hunger, driven out from the community, living in desolate valleys and holes in the rocks (30:1–8). He reports how they make him a song and a byword, keep their distance, and spit in his face (30:9–10). The description of these men is Job’s own, spoken in bitterness and grief; this page reports it soberly and does not draw lessons about the poor beyond what the text says, especially since Job elsewhere grieves for the needy (30:25) and claims to have helped them (29:12–16). He traces their boldness to an act of God, “For he has untied his cord, and afflicted me” (30:11), and then describes the rabble’s assault in images of a siege through a wide breach (30:12–14). Several phrases in 30:11–14 are difficult in Hebrew, and translations differ in detail, so this page does not press them. The unit ends with terrors turned on him and his honor and welfare blown away like wind and cloud (30:15). Both traditions read Job’s words as lament over humiliation, not as a pattern of contempt to imitate.

verses.text: “But now those who are younger than I have me in derision, whose fathers I considered unworthy to put with my sheep dogs.
verses.arminianNotes: “But now those who are younger than I have me in derision.” Arminian readers note the sharp turn from remembrance to present humiliation. Job’s harsh words about their fathers are his own, spoken in bitterness, and are reported here as such.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the pain of a man mocked by those who once deferred to him (29:8). Shared ground: both traditions report Job’s description soberly, without endorsing his contempt or scolding his grief, and see the verse as the start of his lament.

verses.text: Of what use is the strength of their hands to me, men in whom ripe age has perished?
verses.arminianNotes: Job asks what use the strength of their hands could be to him. Arminian readers note that he describes these men as weak and worn out. The point is the depth of his humiliation: even those he considered of no account now scorn him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the verse as heightening Job’s sense of disgrace. Shared ground: both traditions read the description as Job’s perspective in grief, and both avoid drawing broader lessons about the poor beyond what the text says.

verses.text: They are gaunt from lack and famine. They gnaw the dry ground, in the gloom of waste and desolation.
verses.arminianNotes: They are gaunt from lack and famine and gnaw the dry ground. Arminian readers note that Job describes deep poverty and hunger. Readers may notice that these mockers are themselves suffering, even as they add to Job’s suffering.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a picture of destitution in a desolate place. Shared ground: both traditions report Job’s description soberly and with compassion for all who suffer, without treating poverty itself as evidence of wickedness.

verses.text: They pluck salt herbs by the bushes. The roots of the broom tree are their food.
verses.arminianNotes: They pluck salt herbs and eat the roots of the broom tree. Arminian readers note the image of survival on the poorest food. Job’s description emphasizes how far outside ordinary life these men have been driven.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the verse as describing extreme want. Shared ground: both traditions read it as part of Job’s portrait of the mockers’ condition, reported soberly and without adding judgments the text does not make.

verses.text: They are driven out from among men. They cry after them as after a thief,
verses.arminianNotes: They are driven out from among men, who shout after them as after a thief. Arminian readers note that these men are outcasts, rejected by the community. Job, too, now finds himself rejected, though for different reasons.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the outcasts’ rejection and notice the parallel with Job’s own isolation. Shared ground: both traditions report the description soberly and recognize the sorrow of those cast out from community.

verses.text: so that they live in frightful valleys, and in holes of the earth and of the rocks.
verses.arminianNotes: They live in frightful valleys and in holes of the earth and rocks. Arminian readers note the bleakness of their dwelling places. Job describes people living on the edges of habitable land, far from the city gate where he once sat.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the contrast between Job’s former seat at the gate (29:7) and the outcasts’ dwellings. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of Job’s description, reported without adding contempt.

verses.text: They bray among the bushes. They are gathered together under the nettles.
verses.arminianNotes: “They bray among the bushes.” Arminian readers note that Job uses animal imagery to describe these men, a sign of his bitterness. They report the image as Job’s own words without adopting his contempt.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the harshness of Job’s language and recognize it as the speech of a wounded man. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse soberly, neither repeating Job’s contempt nor condemning him for voicing it in grief.

verses.text: They are children of fools, yes, children of wicked men. They were flogged out of the land.
verses.arminianNotes: “They are children of fools, yes, children of wicked men. They were flogged out of the land.” Arminian readers note that this is Job’s judgment on the mockers’ families. It is reported as his speech, not as the book’s settled verdict.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise treat the words as part of Job’s lament and do not extend them into a general judgment. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse soberly and avoid demeaning the poor beyond what Job, in his grief, actually says.

verses.text: “Now I have become their song. Yes, I am a byword to them.
verses.arminianNotes: “Now I have become their song. Yes, I am a byword to them.” Arminian readers hear the pain of public mockery. The man who was once honored at the gate has become the subject of ridicule, and Job feels it deeply.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear honest grief over disgrace and recall similar laments in the Psalms. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse with pastoral compassion for those who suffer mockery and shame.

verses.text: They abhor me, they stand aloof from me, and don’t hesitate to spit in my face.
verses.arminianNotes: They abhor Job, stand aloof, and spit in his face. Arminian readers note the extremity of his humiliation. Spitting in the face was a grave insult, and Job’s report shows how completely his standing has been reversed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the depth of Job’s shame. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as honest lament over cruelty, and both affirm compassion for those who are scorned, without adding details the text does not give.

verses.text: For he has untied his cord, and afflicted me; and they have thrown off restraint before me.
verses.arminianNotes: “For he has untied his cord, and afflicted me.” Arminian readers note that Job attributes his affliction to God, though the image of the cord is obscure. They read his words as the perception of a sufferer, not a complete account of events.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear Job tracing his affliction to God’s hand, as the prologue places his trials under God’s permission. The phrasing is uncertain in Hebrew. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as lament and do not press the difficult image.

verses.text: On my right hand rise the rabble. They thrust aside my feet. They cast their ways of destruction up against me.
verses.arminianNotes: On Job’s right hand rise the rabble, thrusting aside his feet. Arminian readers note that the precise sense of some lines is difficult, but the picture is of hostile people pressing against him and blocking his way.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hold the difficult wording loosely while hearing Job’s sense of being besieged. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of Job’s lament over hostility, without basing conclusions on uncertain phrases.

verses.text: They mar my path. They promote my destruction without anyone’s help.
verses.arminianNotes: “They mar my path. They promote my destruction without anyone’s help.” Arminian readers note that the last phrase is difficult and translations differ. The overall picture is of people who obstruct Job and add to his ruin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise acknowledge the uncertain wording and avoid pressing it. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as Job’s lament over those who make his suffering worse, and both handle the difficult phrasing cautiously.

verses.text: As through a wide breach they come. They roll themselves in amid the ruin.
verses.arminianNotes: “As through a wide breach they come.” Arminian readers note the image of a siege, with attackers pouring through a broken wall. Job feels overwhelmed, as though his defenses have collapsed and hostility rushes in.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the siege imagery as poetry of overwhelming distress. The details are difficult in Hebrew. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as lament, and both decline to build conclusions on obscure lines.

verses.text: Terrors have turned on me. They chase my honor as the wind. My welfare has passed away as a cloud.
verses.arminianNotes: Terrors have turned on Job, and his honor and welfare have blown away like wind and cloud. Arminian readers note the images of transience. What once seemed solid in Job’s life has vanished as quickly as a passing cloud.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the grief of lost honor and security. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as closing this part of Job’s lament, and both see in it the fragility of earthly standing, without scolding Job for mourning its loss.
